title: The Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
plain_title: Weak tracking of subcontractors on health department contracts
agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) properly oversees the subcontractors that its prime vendors hire on health and human services contracts, such as running programs at neighborhood clinics. Auditors examined sampled contracts covering fiscal years 2022 through 2024.
background: DOHMH contracts with non-profit and for-profit providers called prime vendors, which sometimes hire subcontractors of their own, and since the city has no direct contract with subcontractors it relies on agencies to oversee how primes use them. This audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies, launched after watchdog reports found weak oversight of subcontracting on city contracts.

findings.plain: Prime vendors paid about $2.9 million to eight subcontractors that were not approved to work on the sampled contracts. DOHMH said the vendors had been approved, but under the wrong contract numbers.
findings.quote: subcontractors not approved to work on the sampled contracts received about $2.9 million in payments from prime contractors

findings.plain: DOHMH could not fully show it vetted subcontractors. Auditors found insufficient evidence of vetting for two of eight sampled subcontractors that required it, an outdated background questionnaire for one large subcontract and incomplete approval forms for six of 21 subcontracts.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find sufficient evidence for two of the eight sampled subcontractors that DOHMH did this

findings.plain: The agency did not make sure prime vendors got competitive bids. For three of the 13 sampled subcontractors that required a bidding process, there was no evidence three written estimates were obtained.
findings.quote: The auditors found no evidence that three bids were obtained for three of the 13 sampled subcontractors that required a bidding process.

findings.plain: Subcontractors were entered and approved in the city's Payee Information Portal (PIP) far too late. For 19 of 21 sampled subcontractors, recording came 35 to 574 days after work started, and DOHMH's approval came as much as 706 days, almost two years, after the start date.
findings.quote: the vendors recorded the subcontracts in PIP ranging from 35 to 574 days after the subcontract’s start date

findings.plain: Payments to subcontractors were barely recorded in the city system. Prime vendors' ledgers showed $3,691,056 paid to 16 subcontractors, but only about 1% of that was recorded in the Payee Information Portal.
findings.quote: only $35,628 (1%) of these payments were recorded in PIP

findings.plain: DOHMH does not make sure subcontractors get paid on time and has no agencywide process for handling their complaints. Of 18 sampled invoices, 17 were paid 32 to 214 days late, and doulas in a city childbirth support program complained of waiting months for payment.
findings.quote: The auditors found 17 of the 18 invoices were paid late.

findings.plain: Only 5.1% of the money paid to for-profit subcontractors on the sampled contracts, $32,500 of $634,114, went to a certified Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise (M/WBE).
findings.quote: only 5.1% of the monies spent on sampled contracts’ for-profit subcontractors went to Minority and Women-Owned Business Enterprises

numbers.label: Paid to subcontractors not approved on sampled contracts
Longest delay approving a subcontractor in the city portal
Share of subcontractor payments recorded in the city system
For-profit subcontractor spending that went to M/WBEs

recommendations: Make sure payments for subcontracting expenses go only to vendors DOHMH has approved as subcontractors on those specific contracts.

Prevent payments to unapproved subcontractors by carefully reviewing invoices submitted by prime vendors and continue periodically reviewing prime vendors' general ledgers, subcontract agreements and invoices.
Make sure prime vendors submit subcontractor information, including agreements and payment details, in the PASSPort procurement system.
Make all reasonable efforts to ensure the city's Financial Management System accurately reflects subcontractor approvals and industry classifications.
Document the process of vetting and running background checks on proposed subcontractors.
Make sure prime vendors use competitive bidding when selecting subcontractors.
Review subcontract agreements and make sure prime contractors pay their subcontractors promptly.
Consider using more Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise contractors and continue encouraging prime vendors to use more M/WBE subcontractors.
agency_response: DOHMH agreed with six recommendations and called the other two unnecessary, saying it already documents subcontractor reviews and already prioritizes Minority and Women-owned Business Enterprise vendors. Auditors urged the agency to implement both anyway.
implementation_note: Of the seven 2021 Department of Investigation recommendations on subcontractor oversight directed at agencies, the audit found DOHMH had implemented all seven.
